newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sanlam sees new confidence in South Africa economy.
newsitem.headline: Sanlam sees new confidence in South Africa economy.

text.p: Growing confidence in South Africa's economic management could lure back foreign investors frightened off by last year's rand fall, Dries du Toit, Sanlam's head of portfolio management, said in an interview.
"Everybody is now focusing on the (March 12) budget," Du Toit said told Reuters.
"You get the feeling that there is a plan. We don't know the full content, but there is a plan. The Minister of Finance (Trevor Manuel), (Deputy President) Thabo Mbeki, they're working as a team."
Du Toit was speaking four weeks after the mutual insurer's investment unit was transformed into Sanlam Asset Management, with investment chief Hendrik Bester as managing director-deignate.
Bester said doubts about the abilities of the government's finance team appeared to have declined and there was now growing confidence in Manuel.
"For the first time in a long time, they are getting a better handle on everything. They're back in control," he said.
Du Toit said that though this year's unexpectedly quick recovery of the rand against foreign currencies could not be pinned down to any single cause, he was confident that the trend would hold.

He predicted a rand-dollar rate of around 4.80 to 4.85 by the end of 1997 and said the decline from around 4.54 at present could be less than the inflation differential between South Africa and its main trading partners.
South Africa's annual inflation rate increased to 9.4 percent in December, but most economists expect it to remain in single digits on average in 1997.

"The sentiment has changed. We haven't seen an increase in the reserves yet. We haven't seen any economic activity picking up yet. We haven't seen interest rates coming down, except for the money market shortage and the short-term call rate.
"The capital market is a very sensitive barometer of what is going to happen and we are seeing very positive signals right now," he said.
Du Toit said President Nelson Mandela's opening address to the 1997 session of parliament on Friday could set the scene for a further consolidation of the recent gains.
"There are high expectations for the President's speech," he said.
"Privatisation will finally be getting off the ground...it seems to us that there really is a plan to move ahead, even in the first half of this year. There is a new sense of urgency."
Manuel was criticised last year for implementing his macro-economic strategy for job-creating growth too slowly.

Leaders of Mandela's ruling African National Congress resolved at a private meeting earlier this year, however, to work to an undisclosed timetable that would include a relaxation of remaining exchange controls and a renewed commitment to the privatiation of some state-owned assets.

"If (foreign) investors say the rand is undervalued and the fall was overdone then they could come back and if that view is reinforced by the President's speech, the budget and the roadshow of Trevor Manuel they could really start to come back," he said.
Manuel is due to address local financial market participants in Johannesburg and Cape Town on February 20.
